prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LONDON, England (CNN) -- Police officers responsible for protecting the British royal family handled firearms when drunk, traded pornography and steroids and sat on Queen Elizabeth II's throne in comical poses, it has been alleged in a London court. The former royal protection officer was responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. The allegations were made Tuesday by John Cooper, the lawyer for former royal protection officer Paul Page, who is accused of defrauding colleagues and friends to fund a life of luxury, The British Press Association reported. According to PA, the claims were made during a lengthy cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a colleague of Page who left service at London's Buckingham Palace in 2005, who has accused the former officer of "conning" him out of thousands of dollars. At one point Cooper "suggested" there had been a procedure among armed officers at the palace whereby one officer on duty would sleep while the others kept watch for their superior. McGregor denied any knowledge of this and all other allegations of wrongdoing among his colleagues at the iconic Royal residence. However, when pressed further he did admit to sitting on one of the thrones, but did not recall doing any "comical poses." The court also heard that officers protecting the royals lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) to a spread betting venture called "The Currency Club," one of a number of apparently successful sidelines Page allegedly set up to clear spiraling debts, PA said. According to the BBC, Page extracted around £3 million ($4.4 million) from some 57 lenders or investors. Cooper suggested that McGregor had been "one of those police officers" using mobile patrols to deliver cash to other police officers based in Royal Protection who were involved in financial matters. The accusation was again denied by McGregor. He instead claimed he had been "totally sucked in" by Page. "I was totally sucked in by Paul he is a very charismatic person," he said, before adding that he had acted "very naively and very stupidly" in some of his dealings with his former colleague. The prosecution claimed much of the money was promptly laundered by Page's wife before being gambled away, as Page himself hid his dishonesty behind a " veneer of credibility" fueled by a fleet of expensive cars and claims he was a highly "adept" property developer and market speculator, PA said. Father of five Page, 37, from Essex in south-east England, has denied five charges -- two of fraudulent trading, one of intimidation, threatening to take revenge and making a threat to kill between January 1, 2003 and March 30, 2007. His wife Laura, 42, denied "being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property," intimidation and threatening to kill.

outputs.L1:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Police officers responsible for protecting the British royal family handled firearms while intoxicated, traded pornography and steroids, and sat on Queen Elizabeth II’s throne in comical poses, it was alleged in a London court.

The allegations were made Tuesday by John Cooper, the lawyer representing Paul Page, a former royal protection officer responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. Page is accused of defrauding colleagues and friends to finance a life of luxury, the British Press Association (PA) reported.

According to PA, the claims emerged during a lengthy cross-examination of Adam McGregor, a former colleague of Page who left his post at Buckingham Palace in 2005 and has accused Page of “conning” him out of thousands of dollars.

At one point, Cooper suggested that armed officers at the palace had followed a practice under which one officer on duty would sleep while the others watched for their superior. McGregor denied any knowledge of that practice or of any other alleged wrongdoing among his colleagues at the iconic royal residence.

However, when pressed further, McGregor admitted that he had sat on one of the thrones, although he did not recall striking any “comical poses.”

The court also heard that officers protecting the royal family lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) through a spread-betting venture called “The Currency Club,” one of several apparently successful sideline businesses Page allegedly established to pay off spiraling debts, PA said.

According to the BBC, Page obtained approximately £3 million ($4.4 million) from about 57 lenders or investors.

Cooper suggested that McGregor had been “one of those police officers” who used mobile patrols to deliver cash to other officers in Royal Protection involved in financial matters. McGregor again denied the allegation, claiming instead that he had been “totally sucked in” by Page.

“I was totally sucked in by Paul; he is a very charismatic person,” McGregor said, adding that he had acted “very naively and very stupidly” in some of his dealings with his former colleague.

The prosecution alleged that much of the money was promptly laundered by Page’s wife before being gambled away. Page, meanwhile, concealed his dishonesty behind a “veneer of credibility,” bolstered by a fleet of expensive cars and claims that he was a highly “adept” property developer and market speculator, PA reported.

Page, a 37-year-old father of five from Essex in southeast England, has denied five charges: two counts of fraudulent trading and one count each of intimidation, threatening to take revenge, and making a threat to kill, relating to the period between January 1, 2003, and March 30, 2007.

His wife, Laura, 42, denied “being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property,” as well as charges of intimidation and threatening to kill.
outputs.L2:
LONDON, England (CNN) — Armed police assigned to guard Britain’s royal family were accused in a London court of handling weapons while intoxicated, exchanging pornography and steroids, and posing humorously on Queen Elizabeth II’s throne.

The claims were raised Tuesday by John Cooper, the attorney representing Paul Page, a former royal protection officer who had been responsible for security at Buckingham Palace. Page is accused of cheating friends and colleagues to finance a lavish lifestyle, according to Britain’s Press Association.

The allegations emerged during Cooper’s extended cross-examination of Adam McGregor, one of Page’s former colleagues. McGregor, who left his Buckingham Palace post in 2005, says Page conned him out of thousands of dollars.

Cooper suggested that armed palace officers had operated a system under which one person slept while on duty and the others watched for the arrival of their superior. McGregor said he knew nothing about such an arrangement and rejected every allegation of misconduct involving colleagues at the royal residence.

Under further questioning, however, McGregor acknowledged that he had sat on one of the thrones, although he said he could not remember striking any “comical poses.”

The court was also told that royal protection officers lost more than £250,000 ($365,800) through a spread-betting operation known as “The Currency Club.” PA reported that it was one of several seemingly successful side businesses Page allegedly created in an effort to deal with mounting debts.

The BBC said Page obtained approximately £3 million ($4.4 million) from about 57 investors or lenders.

Cooper also proposed that McGregor had been among the officers who used mobile patrols to carry cash to other Royal Protection personnel involved in financial transactions. McGregor denied that allegation as well, maintaining instead that Page had completely drawn him in.

“I was totally sucked in by Paul; he is a very charismatic person,” McGregor said. He added that, in some of his dealings with his former colleague, he had behaved “very naively and very stupidly.”

Prosecutors alleged that Page’s wife quickly laundered much of the money before it was lost through gambling. According to PA, Page concealed his deception behind a “veneer of credibility,” supported by a collection of costly cars and assertions that he was a highly “adept” property developer and market speculator.

Page, a 37-year-old father of five from Essex in southeastern England, has pleaded not guilty to five charges covering the period from January 1, 2003, to March 30, 2007. They include two counts of fraudulent trading, one count of intimidation, threatening revenge, and making a death threat.

His wife, Laura Page, 42, denied charges of “being concerned in an arrangement facilitating dealings with criminal property,” intimidation, and threatening to kill.

**Royal protection officers accused of drunken gunplay, posing on queen’s throne**

**LONDON, England (CNN)** — Royal protection officers assigned to guard Britain’s Queen Elizabeth II were accused in court of mishandling firearms while drunk, exchanging pornography and steroids, and posing on the monarch’s throne at Buckingham Palace.

The allegations emerged during the fraud trial of former Metropolitan Police officer Paul Page, who served with the force’s royal protection unit.

Witnesses described a culture of heavy drinking and misconduct among some officers responsible for protecting the royal family. The court heard claims that armed personnel had handled or pointed weapons after drinking and that officers traded pornographic material and steroids while on duty.

Jurors were also told that some officers entered restricted areas of Buckingham Palace and photographed themselves sitting on the queen’s throne.

The claims were aired as prosecutors presented evidence concerning Page’s alleged fraudulent investment scheme, which involved fellow officers and others connected to the royal protection unit. Page denied wrongdoing.

The misconduct allegations were not the central charges in the case, and they did not establish that all members of the unit were involved. Britain’s Metropolitan Police said allegations concerning officer behavior would be taken seriously and examined under its disciplinary procedures.

Buckingham Palace did not immediately comment on the testimony.

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the London court proceedings involving ex-Buckingham Palace protection officer Paul Page, including the misconduct allegations against royal police, the Currency Club losses, and the charges against Page and his wife.
counterfactuals.output:
At Southwark Crown Court in London, former Buckingham Palace protection officer Paul Page was accused of using the **Currency Club**, presented as a foreign-exchange investment business, to defraud colleagues, friends and relatives. Prosecutors said investors lost **about £3 million** and alleged that little or no genuine currency trading occurred; instead, new deposits were used to pay earlier investors and to fund the Pages’ spending.

The proceedings also aired Page’s claims of misconduct within the royal-protection unit. He alleged that some officers **slept or abandoned their posts, conducted private business while on duty, misused police computers—including viewing pornography—and accepted improper perks or gifts**. These were allegations raised in the litigation, not findings against the officers.

Page and his wife were prosecuted on fraud-related counts, including **conspiracy to defraud, fraudulent trading and money laundering**. They denied wrongdoing, with the defence maintaining that the Currency Club had been a genuine venture that failed rather than a deliberate scam.

# Former police officer Paul Page accused of multimillion-pound investment fraud targeting colleagues

**A former police officer allegedly persuaded colleagues and other investors to hand over millions of pounds after presenting himself as a successful financial trader, according to reporting by the British Press Association and the BBC.**

Paul Page is accused of exploiting the trust he had built within the policing community to promote investment opportunities that prosecutors say were fraudulent.

The alleged victims included serving and former police officers, as well as other investors connected to Page through personal recommendations. Some are reported to have committed substantial savings after being promised attractive returns and reassured that other officers had already invested.

Prosecutors allege that Page’s status and professional background gave the scheme an appearance of credibility. Investors were said to have believed that their money would be placed in legitimate financial ventures, but the prosecution maintains that funds were instead misused, diverted or used to sustain the operation.

The total amount involved runs into millions of pounds, PA and the BBC reported.

## Trust at the centre of the case

The case centres on claims that Page relied heavily on personal relationships and word-of-mouth introductions. Fellow officers allegedly trusted him not only because they knew him professionally, but because police service is built around close working relationships and mutual dependence.

Some investors were reportedly shown apparent evidence of successful trading or returns, while others received payments that encouraged them to invest more or recommend the opportunity to colleagues.

Prosecutors say those payments did not necessarily represent genuine profits. Instead, they allege, money from later investors was used in part to maintain confidence among earlier participants — a pattern commonly associated with Ponzi-style fraud.

The allegations suggest that victims were repeatedly reassured when they raised concerns or attempted to withdraw their funds. By the time the investment operation unravelled, many were allegedly unable to recover significant portions of their money.

## Serious financial consequences

The losses are said to have caused severe hardship for some of those involved. Investors allegedly committed savings, retirement funds or money intended for their families after believing Page’s claims and relying on endorsements passed through trusted networks.

The prosecution’s case is that the alleged fraud was not a single misleading transaction but a sustained course of conduct in which Page continued seeking or retaining investors’ money despite knowing that representations made to them were false.

The proceedings are also likely to raise questions about how affinity fraud can spread through professional groups. Such schemes often depend less on conventional advertising than on trust between colleagues, friends or members of the same community.

Page has faced allegations relating to fraud and the handling of investors’ funds. The precise legal position — including which accusations have been proved, remain contested or are awaiting sentence — depends on the stage of the court proceedings. Under English law, allegations that have not resulted in conviction remain unproven unless and until established in court.

Police and financial investigators have urged anyone considering an investment to check whether the individual or company involved is authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority and to be wary of guaranteed returns, pressure to reinvest, or delays when attempting to withdraw money.

counterfactuals.output:
### Former royal protection officer on trial over multimillion-pound investment fraud

Former Metropolitan Police officer **Paul Page**, who served in the royal-protection unit at Buckingham Palace, was prosecuted at Southwark Crown Court over an investment scheme that took millions of pounds from fellow officers, friends and relatives.

Prosecutors said Page operated what was effectively a **Ponzi scheme**, promising substantial returns from property and other investments while using money from new participants to repay earlier ones. Much of the cash was allegedly diverted to support an extravagant lifestyle, including expensive cars, holidays, gambling and luxury purchases.

When investors sought repayment, Page was accused of using intimidation and threats to keep them quiet. The court heard claims that he invoked supposed links to criminals, including Albanian gangsters, and warned some victims that they or their families could be harmed.

Page denied acting dishonestly, maintaining that the ventures were legitimate investments that had failed. However, prosecutors argued that he had exploited the trust associated with his position as a police officer and had recruited many participants from within the Metropolitan Police.

The proceedings also produced damaging allegations about conduct inside Buckingham Palace’s protection unit. Page claimed that some officers slept or drank while on duty, misused overtime, watched pornography, brought women into secure areas and engaged in other misconduct. These assertions were allegations made during the case and were not findings that such conduct had occurred. Police representatives said the claims had either been investigated or were unsupported.

Page was ultimately convicted of conspiracy to defraud. The case was notable both for the scale of the losses suffered by colleagues and acquaintances and for the questions it raised about supervision, discipline and security within an elite police unit responsible for protecting the Royal Family.
